clinicalPearls: Uterine rupture is a full-thickness disruption of the uterine wall involving the myometrium and overlying serosa, often with the membranes, which may extrude the fetus or placenta into the peritoneal cavity; it is distinguished from dehiscence, a partial scar separation with intact serosa
The commonest setting is labour in a uterus scarred by previous caesarean section, particularly attempted vaginal birth after a previous classical or inverted-T incision

Other risk factors include previous myomectomy or uterine surgery, injudicious use of oxytocin or prostaglandins, obstructed or prolonged labour, grand multiparity, uterine anomaly, trauma, and difficult instrumental delivery
The most consistent and often earliest sign is an abnormal fetal heart rate pattern, particularly a prolonged deceleration or bradycardia

Maternal features include acute scar or abdominal pain that may break through effective regional analgesia, vaginal bleeding, cessation of contractions, loss of the presenting part with a rising station, palpable fetal parts abdominally, haematuria, and signs of hypovolaemic shock
Management is immediate resuscitation and emergency laparotomy with delivery of the fetus, followed by repair of the defect or, when repair is not feasible, hysterectomy
Massive obstetric haemorrhage should be anticipated, so major-haemorrhage protocols, blood products, and senior obstetric and anaesthetic support are essential
The recurrence risk in a subsequent pregnancy influences counselling about mode of delivery, and induction or augmentation of a scarred uterus must be undertaken with caution
reference.pathophysiology: The pregnant uterine wall is subjected to rising intrauterine pressure during contractions. A previous full-thickness scar, or an area weakened by surgery, adenomyosis, or a congenital anomaly, is less elastic and less vascular than surrounding myometrium and can separate under repeated stretching and contraction. When augmentation with oxytocin or prostaglandins produces excessive uterine activity, or when labour is obstructed and the lower segment thins progressively, the wall can give way. Rupture opens uterine vessels, causing haemorrhage into the peritoneum or vagina, and loss of wall integrity abolishes effective contractions and can expel the fetus and placenta from the cavity, abruptly cutting off uteroplacental perfusion. The result is rapid fetal hypoxia and maternal haemorrhagic shock.
additionalDifferentials: Placenta praevia or other antepartum haemorrhage
Other causes of an acute abdomen in pregnancy such as appendicitis or a ruptured viscus
Amniotic fluid embolism causing sudden collapse and fetal compromise
Concealed haemorrhage from another source presenting with hypovolaemic shock
additionalInvestigations: Continuous cardiotocography, since an abnormal fetal heart rate is often the first clue
Urgent clinical abdominal assessment for tenderness, palpable fetal parts, and loss of station
Full blood count, coagulation screen, fibrinogen, and group-and-save or crossmatch
Ultrasound, if time permits, for free intraperitoneal fluid, fetal position, and viability
Urinalysis or catheter specimen for haematuria suggesting bladder involvement or lower-segment extension
Blood gas and lactate to gauge maternal and fetal compromise
redFlags: Prolonged fetal bradycardia or a sudden severe fetal heart rate abnormality in a labouring woman with a scar
Breakthrough scar or abdominal pain despite regional analgesia
Maternal haemodynamic instability or signs of hypovolaemic shock
Cessation of uterine contractions with recession of the presenting part
Palpable fetal parts through the abdominal wall or new haematuria
reference.prognosis: Prompt recognition and immediate operative delivery are associated with maternal survival and, if the fetus is delivered quickly, a reasonable neonatal outcome. Delay leads to fetal hypoxic injury or death and maternal exsanguination, and future pregnancies carry a raised risk of recurrence.
pitfalls: Attributing early fetal heart rate changes to benign causes in a woman attempting vaginal birth after caesarean
Aggressive augmentation of a scarred or obstructed uterus with uterotonics
Misreading breakthrough pain under epidural as merely inadequate analgesia
Underestimating blood loss and activating major-haemorrhage support too late
Failing to counsel about recurrence risk and delivery planning in subsequent pregnancies
references: RCOG Green-top Guideline on birth after previous caesarean birth
Oxford Handbook of Obstetrics and Gynaecology
management: Immediate maternal resuscitation under the major haemorrhage protocol with wide-bore access, crystalloid and blood products
Emergency laparotomy with immediate delivery of the foetus as the definitive management
Surgical repair of the uterine defect where feasible, or hysterectomy when repair is not possible or bleeding is uncontrolled
Neonatal resuscitation team on standby for hypoxic-ischaemic compromise
Senior obstetric and anaesthetic involvement with intraoperative haemostasis and correction of coagulopathy
Prevention through cautious use of oxytocin and prostaglandins and careful selection and monitoring of vaginal birth after caesarean
Counselling about the high recurrence risk with recommendation of planned caesarean before labour in future pregnancies
